rows.text: Honestly, this is a standard sign-in card, so my team would have no trouble with it — email, password, submit. The password-strength countdown and the "Meets the password rules" flip are nice touches that stop the usual back-and-forth. Setting up the authenticator app is described clearly enough with the two numbered steps, so even my less technical coordinators could follow it.

Honestly this looks straightforward — it's a plain sign-in and workspace-creation card, nothing that would trip up me or my team. The disabled-until-filled button, Enter-to-submit, and live password rules are the kind of small conveniences I appreciate, and the MFA and reset flows are laid out step-by-step. I could get my nine people through this without writing a procedure.

The step-by-step rail with plain-language lock reasons and a single primary button per card is the kind of scaffolding my junior associates would actually find approachable, and the auto-save reassures me. What worries me is that it collapses a genuinely multi-week, multi-party process into a linear 10-step wizard — real ANDS work loops back constantly, and I'd need to know I can revisit steps and hand off between team members, which the walkthrough doesn't tell me.

The linear 10-step rail with a "You're here" marker and padlocked future steps is genuinely how I'd want a junior on my team walked through their first filing, so the skeleton is easy to follow. But some of these steps are not things a form can make easy — knowing your Dossier ID format or waiting two weeks on a Company ID enrolment is real friction the software can only surface, not remove. The 3D "tower" and the single "one thing standing between you and ready" framing would help me triage quickly.

Honestly this reads as fairly approachable — the New dossier flow is two fields and the placeholder-ID escape hatch is thoughtful for the common case where Health Canada hasn't issued the ID yet. My team lives in Vault RIM and docuBridge, so a clean tile grid with a status chip and progress bar is legible at a glance. My only friction is that renaming and deleting fall back to native browser prompt/confirm dialogs, which feels clunky and off-brand for a regulated tool.

This looks straightforward enough for someone like me who's spent years in Vault RIM — a catalog of tiles, a "New dossier +" button, two fields. The placeholder-ID path is a thoughtful touch since you rarely have the real Dossier ID when you start prep, and jumping straight into the Module 1 workspace on creation is sensible. I don't love that renaming and deleting fall back on native browser prompts, which feel clumsy and off-brand for a compliance tool.

The three-column layout with a section tree, center authoring, and a readiness rail on the right is a pattern my team already knows from Vault, so navigation wouldn't scare anyone. What worries me on ease is the volume of gating rules up front — the Dossier ID format regex, the required-vs-N/A logic, the mode toggles — that's a lot of small decisions before you've authored a single word. I'd want to see it hands-on, but on paper a junior associate could find their way around Module 1 without much hand-holding.

The three-column layout with a section tree, teach box, and readiness rail is familiar territory for anyone coming from Vault RIM, so I could find my way. What worries me is the volume of upfront constraints — the dossier-ID format rule, the sample-vs-author distinction, the mode toggles — my team of nine would need real training before this is muscle memory. It's not hard so much as it demands attention at every step.

The layout is familiar enough — a section tree, gate flags, and req/opt badges map onto how I already think about an eCTD backbone, so I could find my way around. The chat-to-draft flow itself is simple, but the fact that "Review vs Health Canada" and the fallback "Author" button both live under a completely different mode toggle ("Sample & edit") than where you started drafting would trip up my team constantly.

Navigationally it looks straightforward — a section tree, a work panel, gate flags I recognize conceptually, and a chat box that prompts me for exactly what it needs. My concern is the mode toggle: "Author in-app" then "Draft with AI" versus "Sample & edit" is one layer too many, and the fact that the crucial "Review vs Health Canada" check is buried under the OTHER mode is exactly the kind of thing my team would miss under deadline pressure.

The layout follows the mental model I already have from Vault and docuBridge — module tabs M1-M5, a section tree, sequences with purpose chips — so I'd find my footing quickly. My concern is density: readiness flags, validation card, sequences card and export all live on one right rail, and my junior associates would need a walkthrough before they stopped clicking the wrong thing. The "working: 0001" versus "ACTIVE" sequence distinction is the kind of thing that trips people up under deadline pressure.

The layout is dense but conventional enough that my team could find their way around it — tabs for M1 through M5, a section tree, readiness flags. What worries me operationally is the export path relying on a browser confirm dialog; those are trivial to click through by muscle memory, and the "if the validator is offline, the export proceeds silently without a check" behaviour is exactly the kind of thing that trips up a junior on a Friday afternoon.

The layout is reasonably intuitive for someone who lives in portfolio views all day — summary cards, dossier rows, gate and fee chips read like a RIM dashboard I'd recognize. My real worry is my team of 9: the Correspondence page stacks three dense panels with a lot of vocabulary, and I'd want to see whether a junior associate can navigate the SAL/SDN ingest and Form V register without hand-holding. Medium effort to onboard, not trivial.

The layout follows the mental model I already carry — portfolio at a glance, then registry, then correspondence — so I'd find my way around without much hand-holding. The chip navigation and the toggle-to-reveal forms are conventional enough for my team. My only friction is that a lot is packed onto three pages; a new analyst would need a walkthrough before touching the Form V / NOA register.

The step-by-step guided flow with a step rail, a readiness percentage, and auto-saved sessions looks approachable — for a director who evaluates tools for a team of nine, that lowers the training burden considerably. The dossier ID format enforcement (one letter + 6-7 digits) is exactly the kind of guardrail I'd want, and the placeholder-ID option for products without a REP-issued ID yet is thoughtful. My hesitation is that this is one part described in prose; I can't judge how it behaves under a real 200-document Module 3, which is where these tools usually strain.

The guided step-rail-plus-readiness-chip layout is the kind of thing my junior associates would find approachable, and the placeholder-ID escape hatch is a small mercy for when we're waiting on the REP. But the dossier-ID validation rule is stated correctly, which tells me someone knows the CESG process, so I'd expect the rest to be navigable. The "3D submission tower" gimmick I'd ignore entirely.

This is a standard auth card — email, password, MFA, forgot-password. Nothing here I couldn't do in my sleep; the disabled-until-filled button and Enter-to-submit are the conventions I already expect. The password rule counter and live "meets the rules" feedback are the kind of small touches that keep me from bouncing off a signup, so onboarding itself would take me under a minute.

The sign-in itself is trivial and behaves exactly how I'd expect — disabled button until both fields are filled, Enter-to-submit, live password-rule feedback. The workspace-per-client model maps cleanly onto how I actually work across multiple CRO clients, so I'd be oriented in seconds. Nothing here would slow me down.

For someone who assembles sequences daily, the guided step rail and readiness gate would be genuinely easy to move through — I like that Continue stays disabled until a real gate clears rather than letting me kid myself. My worry is the hard dependencies buried mid-flow: if I don't already have my 5-digit Company ID or a valid Dossier ID, the "continue while it's pending" escape hatch keeps me moving but leaves half-real state I'd have to reconcile later, which in practice is where filings stall.

The 10-step left rail with lock reasons and a "you're here" marker is genuinely easy to follow, and I like that the padlocks tell you why a step is gated instead of just greying out. What I don't love is that several steps assume I already have my 5-digit Company ID and a correctly formatted Dossier ID in hand — for someone new to Health Canada that's a wall, though for me it's routine. The "continue while it's pending" escape hatch is a smart touch so the wizard doesn't dead-end while I wait on OSIP.

Honestly this looks straightforward for someone like me who does document assembly all day. New dossier, two fields, create and you're in Module 1 — that's a low-friction path, and I appreciate that the placeholder-ID option means I'm not blocked waiting on Health Canada to issue the ID before I can start structuring the dossier. The regex validation on the ID pattern is a nice guardrail so I don't fat-finger something.

Honestly this looks easy for me — it's just a catalog of dossiers with a create card, and the fields map to things I deal with daily (Dossier ID, product name). The placeholder-ID escape hatch is a nice touch for when we haven't gotten the ID back from REP yet. My one gripe is that renaming and deleting fall back to native browser prompt/confirm dialogs, which feels cheap and error-prone for something as consequential as re-keying a dossier.

The three-column layout with a section tree, center authoring panel, and readiness rail is familiar enough that I'd navigate it quickly, since it maps roughly to how I move through the CTD in eCTD Office. The section eyebrow with module, section number and required/optional status is exactly the anchoring I need. My one friction point is the sample pre-fill flow: I'd have to consciously hunt down every "sample"-tagged field and overwrite it, which is more manual vigilance than I'd like.

The three-column layout with a section tree, teach box, and readiness rail is basically what I already live in inside eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit, so I'd be at home fast. The upload / author / N-A split per section is sensible, and the Dossier ID format hint (one letter + 6-7 digits) is correct for a Health Canada sequence, which tells me someone knew the domain. My only friction is the sheer number of clicks to get from a dossier tile down to an individual section's form, but nothing here looks hard.

Honestly this looks easy enough for me to operate — section tree, work panel, gate flags on the right, it maps cleanly to how I think in eCTD terms. The chat-to-draft flow is straightforward and the fact that Enter sends and nothing saves until "Use this draft" is sensible. My one friction point is that the "Review vs Health Canada" check lives under a different mode ("Sample & edit") than the one I just drafted in, so I'd have to hunt for it — that's an awkward hop mid-task.

The layout is familiar enough — section tree, work panel, gate flags on the right map roughly to how I think in eCTD terms. The chat drafting itself is dead simple to operate: type context, hit Send, click "Use this draft." My real friction is that the important next step — reviewing the draft against Health Canada requirements — is stashed under a completely different mode ("Sample & edit"), so after I save I'd be hunting for it. That's an unnecessary detour on something I'd do 15 times a sequence.

Honestly this looks fairly usable for someone who does eCTD work daily — the sequence card with purpose chips, working-sequence indicator, and per-sequence export is close to how I think. The readiness flags (Documents/Fee/Valid eCTD) and the pre-computed structural check are a nice at-a-glance layer. My one friction point is the "Show all 12 errors" toggling and truncated warnings; when I'm clearing findings I want the full list sortable/filterable by rule code, not paged five at a time.

Honestly this looks usable for someone who does this daily. The sequence card with purpose chips, working-sequence indicator, and "Make active" maps cleanly to how I actually manage lifecycle in eCTD Office, and the readiness flags (Documents/Fee/Valid eCTD) give me a fast at-a-glance triage. The one friction point is that deeper PDF conformance sits behind a separate "Run full check" button, so I'd have to remember to run it before every export rather than it being automatic.

Mechanically this looks easy enough for someone like me — the layout is familiar, chips and forms, register-a-product, ingest a notice, file Form V. I do this kind of tracking daily in eCTD Office and SharePoint, so toggling a form or ticking a checklist is nothing. My only friction is that a lot of distinct regulatory concepts are crammed into three pages, so I'd want to poke around before trusting where each thing lives.

Honestly this looks straightforward to operate — the portfolio-to-registry-to-correspondence flow maps cleanly to how I already think about a portfolio, and the chip navigation is obvious. The registry form with a DIN digit-count hint and the "leave blank until NOC" note tells me someone who's actually done this designed it. My only friction is guessing which page owns what, but that's a five-minute learning curve for someone at my level.

Structurally this reads like something I could pick up fast — a step rail with journey stages, M1–M5 tabs with pass/todo/N-A markers, and a readiness percentage is close to how I already think in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit. The dossier-ID validation (one letter + 6–7 digits) matches the real REP/CESG format, which tells me whoever built this actually knows the process. My only friction is that I do document assembly hands-on all day, so I'd want to see the actual granule/leaf-level authoring, not just tiles in a 3D tower.

The guided step-rail-plus-readiness layout looks approachable, and I appreciate that the dossier ID format is validated up front instead of failing me later. But honestly, for someone who does document assembly daily, the hand-holding "every term explained in plain language" framing feels aimed at a novice, not at me. What I actually need to know — can I import my existing eCTD structure, granularity, leaf handling — isn't mentioned anywhere here.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — it's just an email and password on one card, and the disabled button until both fields are filled is the kind of thing I'm used to. The password rule counting down as I type would help me not fumble, and Enter-to-submit is a small thing but I'd actually use it. I don't think I'd need a senior to walk me through signing in.

Honestly this part looks straightforward — it's just a sign-in and workspace setup, which is the kind of thing I do every day with our shared drive and email logins. The disabled-until-filled button and Enter-to-submit are nice small touches, and the password rule counting down as I type means I wouldn't have to guess. Setting up MFA looks a touch fiddly with the secret code and otpauth stuff, but there's a "Copy setup link" so I'd manage.

The step-by-step left rail with 10 numbered steps and locked-but-explained future steps feels approachable, and I like that later steps unlock only when a gate clears so I can't skip ahead by accident. What worries me is the front-loaded dependencies I don't control: needing a 5-digit Company ID (or a two-week wait after emailing a template) and a correctly formatted Dossier ID before I can really move. For a first-time filer like me, I'd probably still need a senior sitting next to me to get past those early steps.

Honestly this looks fairly approachable for someone at my level — the 10-step left rail and the "You're here" marker mean I always know where I am, which is more than my Word templates give me. The plain-language lock reasons and the single "the thing standing between you and ready" resume button would keep me from feeling lost. My one worry is the sheer number of gates and forms; the first couple of steps look easy, but I'd still be nervous filling in pathway routing on my own.

Honestly this looks pretty manageable — it's just tiles and a "New dossier +" button, which is way less intimidating than the Word templates I fight with on the shared drive. The placeholder-ID option is a relief because on my current filing I've been stuck waiting on the actual Dossier ID and didn't know how to start without it. I'd probably poke around fine on my own.

Honestly this looks pretty manageable — it's just a couple of tiles and a "New dossier" button, nothing intimidating. I like that if I don't have a Dossier ID yet I can start with a placeholder and set the real one later, because I never have the ID at the point I want to start drafting. The one letter + 6-7 digits validation is clear enough that I wouldn't fumble it.

Honestly it looks manageable once someone shows me the three-column layout, but there's a lot on screen at once — module tabs, section tree, right-rail flags, provenance chips. The pre-filled sample with "edit every field" is nice because I'm not staring at a blank form, though I'd be nervous about which fields I still need to touch. The Dossier ID format rule (one letter + 6-7 digits) is the kind of thing I'd normally have to ask a senior about, so having it spelled out inline is genuinely helpful.

Honestly this looks like a lot to take in at once — three columns, module tabs, section glyphs, readiness flags all on one screen. But the "Author in-app" form with pre-filled fields would be way faster than starting from a blank Word template, and I like that the section tells me exactly which one I'm in (M1, 1.2.5). I'd need a senior to walk me through my first dossier, but after that I think I could manage.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable — it's just a chat box where you type in the submission details and it asks you for what it needs, which feels a lot less intimidating than staring at a blank Word template. The mode toggle between "Draft with AI" and "Sample & edit" confused me a bit though, and I don't love that the "Author" fallback button lives under a different tab than where I'd be looking.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable — it's just a chat box with an example prompt showing me exactly what to type, and the "req/opt" badges and progress bar tell me what's still outstanding. What worries me is knowing when to stop chatting: it says the AI asks for details instead of leaving blanks, but I'm still learning what a section actually requires, so I wouldn't always know if it asked me enough. The three tabs (Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A) plus two sub-modes (Draft with AI vs Sample & edit) is a bit of a maze for something I'd use once or twice.

Honestly the layout sounds manageable once someone shows me where things live, but there's a lot on one screen at once, tiles, tabs M1 to M5, a section tree, three cards stacked on the right rail. As a junior I'd be nervous about clicking the wrong thing, especially "Make active" on a sequence, without knowing what it does. The export button being right there is easy, but that ease is exactly what worries me.

Honestly the screen sounds pretty busy — module tabs, a section tree, three cards stacked in a side rail, toggles for showing errors. I think I'd find my way around after someone walked me through it once, but on my own first ANDS I'd be nervous about missing something. The one-click Export beside each sequence is nice and simple though.

Honestly this looks like a lot going on at once — three separate pages, chips across the top, and each dossier row is packed with a module tower, gate chip, fee chip, sometimes a litigation clock. I think once someone showed me where things live I'd be fine, but reading it cold I'd be nervous about clicking the wrong transition button. The forms themselves (Register product, Log correspondence) look straightforward enough for me to fill in.

Honestly it looks like a lot of surfaces to hold in my head at once — Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, plus three stacked panels inside Correspondence. The chips and "Open →/Viewer" links seem straightforward enough, and the register-product form is a normal form I could fill in. But the notice-ingest step (SAL/SDN/NOC, response windows, Form V/NOA) is where I'd be slow and nervous, because I'd be guessing at which type to pick.

Honestly this looks approachable for someone at my level — the three-column layout with a step rail and a "34% ready" chip is the kind of hand-holding I'd want, since right now I'm just juggling Word templates and pinging my seniors. The one place I'd stumble is the Dossier ID: I'd have to already know it's "one letter + 6–7 digits" via a REP request through CESG, and I don't fully understand CESG yet, so I'd probably use the placeholder option and hope that's okay.

Honestly this reads like it'd hold my hand more than my Word templates do, which is a relief — a step rail, one card at a time, and a readiness percentage means I always know where I am. The one thing that already trips me is the Dossier ID rule; I don't have my IDs memorized and I'd have panicked at "one letter + 6–7 digits" if the placeholder option weren't right there. So mostly easy, with a couple of Health-Canada-specific gates I'd need a senior to walk me through the first time.

Honestly, this looks straightforward enough to get into — email, password, a Sign in button that stays greyed out until I've filled both fields. That kind of guardrail I appreciate. The password-strength counter and the "codes rotate every 30 seconds" hint mean I'm not left guessing, which is where most tools lose me. I'd have no trouble getting past this front door.

The sign-in itself looks about as simple as any tool I use — two fields, a button that won't light up until they're filled, Enter to submit. That part I could hand to anyone. The MFA enrollment with the secret code and otpauth URI is where a less technical colleague of mine would get stuck, but for a gatekeeping step I'm actually fine with a little friction.

The step-by-step rail with plain-language lock reasons is the kind of hand-holding I'd actually welcome, since I sign off on submissions rather than assemble them daily. But a few things would slow me down: I still need to know my 5-digit Company ID and the Dossier ID format cold, and the real content work happens on a separate Module builder page, so I'm bouncing between screens. The 3D "tower" is decoration I'd ignore.

The step-by-step rail with 10 steps, plain-language lock reasons, and a single primary button per card looks manageable even for someone like me who doesn't live in these tools all day. What worries me is the front-loaded external dependencies — needing my 5-digit Company ID and a properly formatted Dossier ID up front — because in practice those become the blockers that stall people, and the "continue while it's pending" escape hatch feels like it could let me build on sand.

Honestly the basic flow reads simple enough — I can see a list of my product files, hit "New dossier," type an ID and a product name. That part I could manage. Where I'd slow down is the terminology and knowing whether I've done it correctly; I'd want to click through it once with someone who knows it before I trusted myself to set one up alone.

The basic mechanics look simple enough - a list of dossiers, a button to make a new one, click a tile to open it. I appreciate that the Dossier ID pattern is validated up front and that there's a placeholder path for when you don't yet have the real ID from Health Canada. What gives me pause is relying on native browser prompt and confirm boxes for renaming and deleting - those little dialogs are easy to misread or dismiss by accident.

Honestly the three-column layout with a section tree, glyphs, and a right rail of readiness flags looks manageable — it mirrors how I already think about a submission checklist. What worries me is the volume of small conventions to learn (the �or◐or✓ glyphs, the "sample" tags, the dossier-ID format rule) before I'd feel fluent, and I'd want a proper SOP written around it before letting my team touch it.

Honestly, the three-column layout with a section tree, center panel, and readiness rail is roughly how I already work in our vault, so the mental model isn't foreign to me. But there's a lot going on at once, and small glyphs like the half-filled circle and the "N/A" symbol would slow me down until someone walked me through them. The Dossier-ID format rule (one letter + 6-7 digits) is the kind of precise constraint I appreciate, though I'd want to confirm it matches Health Canada's actual dossier numbering.

Honestly, the layout looks reasonable — a section tree with req/opt badges and a gate rail is the kind of checklist view I'd want. But the idea of drafting a regulatory document by chatting with an AI in a box is not how I work; I assemble and sign, I don't converse. The "Use this draft" step is at least a clear stopping point I understand.

Honestly, the chat part looks simple enough — type what the submission is, read the reply, click "Use this draft." But the flow bothers me: the thing that tells me to run "Review vs Health Canada" is buried under a different mode ("Sample & edit"), and even the fallback "Author" button when the AI isn't configured is somewhere other than where the message points. That kind of mislabeling is exactly what trips up my staff mid-task.

Honestly, this looks like a lot of cards and chips crammed onto one screen, and I'd need someone to walk me through it the first few times. The sequence and validation concepts I know from eCTD, so the layout isn't foreign, but "working: 0001" versus an ACTIVE badge versus "Make active" is the kind of state juggling where I'd make a mistake. It's not point-and-sign simple, which is what I'm used to.

Honestly, the layout looks busy — module tabs, a section tree, three side cards all stacked, and I'd need someone to walk me through it the first time. That said, the core act of reading a status badge and clicking Export beside a sequence is simple enough that I could probably manage the sign-off step without touching the assembly.

Honestly, there's a lot packed onto these three pages, but the flow reads like it follows how I actually work — a portfolio overview, then registry, then correspondence. The chips and buttons are labelled in plain language ("Register product", "Log correspondence", "File Form V"), so I could probably find my way without much hand-holding. My worry is the density: notice types, day-counters, and litigation clocks all on screen at once could overwhelm a junior on my team before they learn the terms.

Honestly, this looks manageable for someone like me — it's mostly reading dashboards and clicking transition buttons, not assembling anything from scratch. The chips and status counts ("Ready to file", "Blocked", "3/7 modules") are the kind of at-a-glance view I'd want when I'm signing off on other people's work. What I can't judge from a walkthrough is how much hidden state sits behind those buttons, and whether a wrong click on "→ Marketed" is reversible.

Honestly, the front door looks manageable — "Start my submission" with a step rail and a readiness percentage is the kind of guided flow I'd want, since I'm the one signing off, not assembling. Where it gets hard is the dossier creation: I'd have to already know the "one letter + 6-7 digits" ID format and that it comes from a REP request through a CESG account, and if I don't have that yet I'm relying on a placeholder d-prefixed ID, which makes me nervous about carrying a fake identifier through a real filing.

On paper this looks manageable — a start button, a step rail, a saved session you can resume. But I'd want to see it before I believe "easy." The dossier ID validation worries me a little: if my staff don't already know the e123456 format they'll hit an error wall, though the placeholder option is a sensible escape hatch. For someone at my comfort level, the guided step-by-step framing is reassuring, but the 3D "submission tower" reads like decoration I'd have to look past.

Honestly this is a bog-standard sign-in card, so no, it wouldn't slow me down at all — email, password, done, and Enter submits. The workspace-per-client model maps cleanly onto how I actually work, since I keep each of my sponsors walled off anyway. The one thing I'd fumble is the MFA setup: "Copy setup link" for an otpauth URI assumes I know to paste it into an authenticator, and my medium-tech clients would stall there.

This part looks straightforward — it's a standard sign-in and workspace-creation card, nothing I'd struggle with. The disabled-until-filled button, live password rule feedback, and Enter-to-submit are the conventions I already expect. Setting up MFA from the Account page and copying an otpauth link is well within my comfort even though I'm only medium-tech.

The step-by-step rail with plain-language lock reasons is genuinely helpful, and I appreciate that it doesn't pretend the Company ID and Dossier ID appear instantly. What worries me is the volume packed into ten steps for someone medium tech comfort — the 3D tower and readiness card are decoration I'd click past to get to the form. My clients would need me holding their hand through the first pass regardless.

The step-by-step spine is easy enough to follow on paper, and I appreciate that it doesn't pretend the Company ID and Dossier ID appear by magic — the "I've requested it, continue while pending" control matches the real two-week wait I've lived through. But the content step punts me to a separate Module builder on another page, and bouncing between the journey and the dossiers page is exactly where my clients lose the thread.

This is straightforward enough for me — a catalog of dossier tiles with a "New dossier +" button is about as simple as it gets, and I'd be creating and opening files without much fuss. The placeholder-ID shortcut is a nice touch for the early-stage clients who haven't filed their Dossier ID Request yet. My only friction is the native browser prompt/confirm dialogs for renaming and deleting, which feel unpolished for a regulatory tool.

Honestly this reads as fairly easy — the New dossier flow is two fields and a button, and the placeholder-ID escape hatch is thoughtful for the reality that clients often haven't filed their Dossier ID Request yet. What would slow me down is that renaming and deleting fall back to native browser prompt and confirm boxes; typing a Dossier ID blind into a JavaScript prompt, with no format echo or validation until after I hit OK, is exactly the kind of thing that produces fat-finger errors on a permanent file identifier.

The three-column layout with a section tree, center authoring panel, and a readiness rail on the right is a sensible mental model, and I'd find it familiar because it mirrors the eCTD structure I already navigate. What worries me on ease is the sheer number of states and glyphs to decode at once, and I'd want to know that the Dossier ID format ("one letter + 6-7 digits") actually matches the current e-number convention rather than a guess.

If I can get past the Dossier ID gate, the three-column layout with a section tree and a right-rail checklist is close to how I already work off my own paper checklists, so navigating would come naturally. The "sample & edit" pre-fill worries me on ease grounds though — I'd spend real time hunting down every sample-tagged field to make sure I didn't leave a worked example in, which is more cognitive load than starting from an empty form.

The layout itself is familiar enough — a section tree, a work panel, gate flags for Documents, Fee, and eCTD validity is more or less how I already think about a dossier. But the chat-drafting path buries too much: I'd get a document saved and not realize the "Review vs Health Canada" check lives under a completely different mode toggle. Making me hunt for the review step after drafting is exactly the kind of workflow gap that trips up busy people.

Mechanically this looks easy enough — click a section, pick "Author in-app", type what I know about the sponsor, and a draft streams back. That mirrors how I already work: I dig the facts out of my checklist and paste them in. My worry is the "Review vs Health Canada" step is buried under a different mode toggle ("Sample & edit"), so the one thing I actually need to do — check required elements against guidance — is the thing I'm most likely to miss.

Structurally this looks manageable for me — tiles, module tabs, readiness flags, and a validation card in the side rail is a layout I could learn quickly. But the sequences workflow with "working: 0001", "Make active", and creating new sequences by purpose is where a less experienced preparer will stumble; that concept trips people up in real eCTD tools and I'd want to see it hand-held better.

The layout is familiar enough — tiles, module tabs, a readiness summary — and the CA-E/CA-W finding codes with a first-5-then-expand toggle is how I'd actually work a validation report. What would slow me down is the "Run full check (PDF conformance)" being a separate manual button; I'd want to know whether structural PASS without running that deep check gives me a false sense of security before I get halfway to export.

Honestly, the layout reads like something I could pick up quickly — a portfolio table with gate and fee chips is the sort of at-a-glance view I build in my own checklists, so the mental model is familiar.
